speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER-FORM AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Before questions are called perhaps hon. members will allow me to say just a word about questions as this is a matter which affects all of us, as respects both time and expense. I am sure hon. members

have felt, as I have sometimes, a little bit annoyed at questions being called and then being allowed to stand, this continuing from week to week and occasionally from month to month. This has been due to the fact that some questions require a great deal of research before they can be answered. Many are standing on the order paper which might well be made orders for returns.
It is obvious that the question of time is important in getting into the business of the afternoon. If the time required for questions could be abbreviated it would be to the advantage of everyone.
There is also the question of the expense involved in preparing answers to some of the questions. It may surprise hon. members to know that that expenditure runs into very considerable figures, particularly in the preparation of returns. The house has from time to time drawn attention to the desirability of limiting rather than increasing the number of civil servants, but to answer many of these questions and to prepare returns involves bringing on additional staffs. That is one of the considerations which should be taken account of by members in preparing questions and notices of motion for which they wish to have returns.
I thought it desirable to ask the Clerk of the House, who is an authority on these matters, to give me a memorandum which I could read to hon. members so that they will not mistake the intention or purpose of the ministry where in answer to questions ministers may feel obliged to say that they have such-and-such information but cannot give more. Because a minister has not answered all that is asked for in a question is no reason why the question should stand. We have to take the responsibility for the answers we give. They may not be satisfactory, and exception may be taken to that fact, but the government itself must decide what answer it shall give to different questions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I now read this memorandum which I have received from the Clerk of the House, who is an authority on the rules and procedure of the house. The memorandum is as follows:
Members of the House of Commons are entitled under standing order 44 to place questions on the order paper seeking information from the ministers of the crown relating to public affairs. The rule does not compel ministers to answer but it says that in replying no facts are to be stated except so far as may be necessary. The rule also provides that no debate is allowed on the answer to a question.
It is a mistake to believe that any kind of question dealing with government business may be asked on the floor of the house. All the authorities such as Hatsell, May, Redlich, Cushing, Todd and Bourinot agree that unless certain rules are observed considerable time can be wasted in putting and answering injudicious questions.
The practice now followed with regard to questions in the house does not conform with parliamentary procedure as observed in other British parliaments. It has been decided in the United Kingdom house that a question cannot be placed on the order paper if it seeks information set forth in documents equally accessible to questioner, as statutes, published reports, et cetera. When questions seeking information published in public documents are placed on the order paper in the United Kingdom, the minister concerned replies by giving the title of the document or blue book in which this information can be found. All printed government reports are distributed free of charge to members of the house.
A rule on which the United Kingdom house is very firm is that questions are inadmissible when they deal with matters referred to a parliamentary committee. This rule does not deprive the member of his rights or privileges; it merely places him in the right channel for procuring proper information.
Public interest at large should be the guiding principle in publishing information on government matters. It seems unfair to the taxpayers of the country that thousands of dollars be spent in the preparation of answers on matters that have only a local interest.
In many cases a letter to a minister or deputy minister would be sufficient for the member to get all the facts required. The purpose of a question, as "May" says, is to obtain information or press for action, and it should not be in effect a short speech or 'limited to giving information or framed as to convey a particular point of view. The rules of the house are so framed as to allow every member to use his right of being informed as to management of public affairs, but it must be understood that in a house of 245 members it is desirable that certain rules be observed lest parliamentary procedure degenerate in confusion and chaos.
That is the end of the memorandum. I place it on Hansard in order that hon. members may not feel that when a minister considers it necessary to answer a question briefly or to draw attention to the fact that certain expenditures will be involved in answering the question, it may not be the thought that the government is seeking to do other than to meet the wishes of hon. gentlemen opposite. All we are seeking to do is to save time and to save expense.
May I add this further word, and this applies to notices of motion for the production of papers. The government should not be expected to be in the position of a reference library to gather together information for members which they are in a position to gather for themselves.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER-FORM AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: If the Prime Minister will permit a supplementary question on the statement he has just read, the authorities cited are nearly all British authorities, and I would ask whether they apply equally to this parliament, since our method of question and answer is fundamentally different from theirs. Members of the British parliament may put a question and then two supplementaries are permitted. It is much the same with research. The members here have few facilities for research, and the purpose of many of the questions is to seek information that would require a great deal of research on the part of a private member. I have often wondered whether facilities should not be granted to private members to get some research work done for them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER-FORM AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, where there is no specific rule
House of Commons-Questions

to the contrary we follow the practice of the United Kingdom parliament. The memorandum which I have just read, in pointing out that the United Kingdom parliament follows a certain procedure upon which authorities are agreed was meant only as a general guide to the house. I am not stating that that is the precise rule we should follow, but that wTe seek to follow their practice in so far as it is advantageous for us so to do. In the British house, as I recollect, questions are put on the order paper which are answered in the same manner as our questions placed on the order paper are answered. The only questions that are allowed in addition to questions on the order paper when they have been answered are questions arising out of those answers. No new questions at all except by special arrangement with the Speaker in advance are allowed as is frequently done here. Further questions, as my hon. friend has said, are limited to supplementary questions.
As to the matter of research, I think the government would be only too ready to provide facilities where it is obviously desirable and possible that those facilities should be granted. But there can be a great abuse of the advantage of using the public service to gather information where that information is intended for local rather than national purposes. I am just suggesting that all hon. members take these factors into consideration.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER-FORM AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister if we might not adopt in some modified form, to meet the conditions of this parliament, the system which is followed in the old land? Actually what the Prime Minister says is partly true, but I think he might go a little farther. As I recall it, what happens in Britain is this. The question is first put on the order paper. This opens the avenue for further questions. The question which is first put on the order paper is not the main question at all; it is simply a lead, and then supplementary questions which are the real kernel of the nut are asked afterwards. It seems to me that something of the kind might be done to help us here; because whether by design or by accident this government has fewer questions directed to it than are directed to most governments under similar circumstances.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER-FORM AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member is quite right in saying that questions put on the order paper in the United Kingdom are put there with the intention of opening the avenue to supplementary ques-

tions. They are put there to get an answer to those questions specifically. If the answer given is satisfactory there will be no supplementary questions at all. The important point is this: the purpose of having questions put on the order paper in the first instance is that the ministry may prepare itself for any additional questions that may be asked. In other words the ministry will not have to answer offhand any questions which may be asked on the orders of the day but will have an opportunity to become in advance fully informed in the event of any supplementary questions being asked in regal'd to any questions on the order paper.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER-FORM AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: Urgent questions do not have to go on the order paper.

speechtext:
These questions have not been answered until now because to answer them without giving the background of the transaction might well be misleading. There is the further reason that announcement of a new long-range transport plane travels around the world, and it did not seem desirable to give any information about a new

Questions
plane until all the information was complete. I shall now ask the indulgence of the house to make a statement on the entire transaction which will, I think, answer all the questions relating to the matter which are on the order paper.
The aircraft plant at Cartierville, P.Q., was constructed by the dominion government in 1942, for the production of P.B.Y. (Catalina) and P.B.Y. (Canso "A") types of amphibian aircraft, in response to an urgent demand for aircraft of this type from the R.C.A.F. and from the air services of the United States, it being represented that important operational assignments made the procurement of these planes imperative. A total of 340 P.B.Y. aircraft were produced at the plant between September, 1943, and March, 1945, and in addition, 29 P.B.Y. aircraft were assembled, at St. Hubert, from parts built at Cartierville. A further 119 hulls and 172 centre sections were built at Cartierville and shipped as components to the United States. The first aircraft were delivered within nine months of the start of production. This was a remarkable feat for a group of working men and women who had little or no experience in aircraft manufacture. It will be seen from the production schedule, which I will ask to have printed in Hansard, that the aircraft were produced at a satisfactory rate, and that substantially more than half of the production was purchased iby the United States government.
The total cost of the facilities at Cartierville, including land, buildings, plant, machinery and tooling, amounts to $21,825,777.33.
Early in 1944, it became apparent that additional orders for P.B.Y. types would not be forthcoming. It was imperative that plans be made either for closing the plant and laying off some 8,000 skilled workers then in employment, or alternatively that another type of aeroplane should be undertaken. Requirements for fighter planes for the R.C.A.F. were well in hand, but both R.C.A.F. and Trans-Canada Air Lines had substantial requirements for long range transport planes. The stated requirement of R.C.A.F. for long range transport was then a minimum of 50 aircraft, and for TCA, a minimum of twenty-five aircraft. At that time, practically all four-engine long range transport planes were being built in the United States, and, of course, the Douglas C-54 was generally considered to be the best. An extensive study was made by Canadian engineers, in collaboration with Douglas and Rolls Royce, to determine the type of plane best suited to Canadian requirements. The conclusion was that the commercial adaptation of the Douglas C-54, known as the DC-4, powered 83166-99
with Rolls Royce engines, would be the aircraft peculiarly well adapted to Canadian service and commercial air line requirements.
The government therefore negotiated with the Douglas Aircraft Company, and secured a licence agreement under which Douglas undertook to furnish plans of its DC-4 type, as well as its DC-6 type then being designed, and to assist in the development, redesign and construction in Canada of an aircraft based on Douglas designs and fitted with Rolls Royce power plants. In this arrangement,'the Rolls Royce Company cooperated fully. The negotiations were completed in the fall of
1944.
The Cartierville plant had been built and managed for the crown, under a management agreement, by Canadian Vickers Limited, who had additional aircraft facilities at St. Hubert. Later, in 1944, the Canadian Vickers Company was engaged in an extensive shipbuilding programme for the allied navies and the merchant service, which involved heavy financial commitments. It was considered advisable to ask Canadian Vickers to divest itself of its management responsibilities related to the Cartierville plant, and to devote its full resources to shipbuilding. The government then entered into a management contract with a group of men who were at that time in charge, for Canadian Vickers, of the management of the Cartierville plant. These men formed a corporation, under the name of Canadair Limited, as a privately-owned management company, charged with the exclusive duty of operating the Cartierville plant as agents of the crown for the production of transport aircraft, as well as to carry out further commitments such as subcontracts for the United States navy for the production of P.B.Y. hulls and centre sections. These latter orders engaged the facilities at Cartierville until March, 1945. During the same period, engineering and tooling for the Canadian transport plane was advanced as rapidly as possible, having regard to the fact that Canadair, Douglas, and Rolls Royce were then filling important war commitments.
After the end of the European war in May
1945,	United States subcontracts were terminated. Employment at Cartierville was then maintained by accepting contracts from commercial air lines in Canada, the United States, South America, and Europe to meet a desperate peacetime need for transport equipment. Engineering and tooling for our four-engine plane had not reached the point where facilities at the plant could be fully employed, and therefore orders were accepted from more

Questions

than 16 commercial operators for the conversion of United States Army Dakota type transports to the commercial DC-3 type. The work involved stripping down army planes and practically rebuilding them into transport types, almost the equivalent of building a new aeroplane. This work commenced in the early summer of 1945 and is still in progress. Up to the middle of September 1946, 87 DC-3 aircraft had been delivered, and this work is still continuing. The integration of these various programmes enabled a high level of employment to be maintained at Cartierville, and also enabled the plant to retain the services of trained personnel for the production, in due course, of a programme of four-engine transport planes.
The first four-engine transport plane, named the North Star, left the assembly line in June, 1946, less than two years after the programme was initiated. This prototype has performed satisfactorily, and has fulfilled the expectations of the group that planned the new plane. A total of seveD finished aircraft have been produced to date, and it is expected that TCA will operate six of these planes in its regular transatlantic service on or about April 1st, 1947.
Out of several long range transport planes planned by manufacturers in the United States and the United Kingdom at about the same time, some of them earlier, only one is in operation to date, namely the Lockheed Constellation. Operational experience with that plane has not been altogether satisfactory, resulting in its being grounded for periods on two occasions. The Canadian plane being the second postr-war transport plane, it was felt that exhaustive tests under all conditions of weather should be made before the plane was put in operation. These have been conducted during the winter months, and minor modifications have resulted. It is worthy of note that ours is the second post-war plane to go into operation. Not a bad record for Canada.

During 1946, the Electric Boat Company, a substantial American corporation, became interested in the Cartierville project. This company, with large financial resources, had examined carefully into Canadian economic conditions, and became convinced that it could wisely and profitably engage some of its liquid capital in Canada. After extensive negotiations, Electric Boat Company acquired substantially all of the stock of Canadair Limited, and has entered into an agreement with the Canadian government, effective as of September- 14, 1946, covering the crown facilities, contracts, etc., at Cartierville. The main features of the agreement are as follows:
(a)	Electric Boat Company to provide Canadair Limited with 82,000,000 working capital forthwith;
(b)	Canadair Limited to waive all claim or right to fees or profits from the beginning of its operations to and including September 14, 1946;
(c)	Canadair Limited to buy at book value the assets of the project, as at September 14, 1946, exclusive of plant, tools and automotive equipment, and to assume the liabilities as set out on the balance sheet of the project prepared as of that date;
(d)	Canadair Limited to buy such automotive equipment as it might require, at prices to be agreed upon with War Assets Corporation;
(e)	Canadair Limited and the government to enter into a fifteen-year lease-option agreement covering the plant facilities and tools, under which the company will pay a fixed annual rental of 8200,000, and will have an option to acquire all of the facilities, including the tools, at an inclusive price ranging from $4,000,000 in the first year to $2,511,961 in the 15th year;
(f)	Of the assets to be purchased by the company, a balance of $3,886,821.10 to be paid for in equal quarterly instalments from June 30, 1947 to December 31, 1948, with interest on the unpaid balance at the rate of 3J per cent per annum;
(g)	The government to assign to Canadair Limited its licence agreement with the Douglas Aircraft Company;
(h)	Canadair to agree to sell to the government and Trans-Canada Air Lines 24 R.C.A.F. type and 20 T.C.A. type aircraft at negotiated fixed prices of $630,000 and $660,000 each respectively, sales tax extra.
Before entering into this agreement, the Department of Reconstruction and Supply satisfied itself that this company is able to provide capable and experienced management for the plant. Mr. W. Oliver West, an early officer of T.C.A., who had since become manager of operations of the Boeing plant at

Questions
Seattle, and had been in responsible charge of the gigantic war production of Boeing, was designated as president of Canadair. The government is satisfied that the present Canadair Company is providing expert and experienced management for the Cartierville property.
Shortly after the war ended, requirements of both the R.C.A.F. and T.C.A. were revised downward. The present requirement of R.C.A.F. is for 24 aeroplanes and for T.C.A., 20 aeroplanes. This reduction in requirements has of course added to the cost of each individual plane, although the cost of the planes is still well below the cost of purchasing and importing into Canada planes of competitive type.
I will now table a statement showing aeroplanes produced each month from the Cartierville plant, together with a list of purchasers of DC-3 conversions. I would ask that these tables be printed in Hansard.
I believe that this statement answers all questions regarding this matter now standing on the order paper.

speechtext:
I am told it is not the practice for the Minister of Justice to give legal advice to the House of Commons. When legal advice is given to the house, he merely passes on what the law officers of the crown have decided, instead of giving his own opinion. I am told that is the practice in parliament. However, I shall add my own opinion. I think on most occasions it will oe the same as that of the deputy minister.
The memorandum of the deputy minister, as furnished to me, is as follows:
Ottawa, March 20, 1947.
Memorandum for Minister of Justice Re Bill 25
You asked for an opinion as to the constitutional validity of the proposed agricultural products act now under consideration by the House of Commons.
Clauses 3 and 4 of the bill merely authorize the Minister of Agriculture, pursuant to agreements between Canada and the governments of other countries for the sale or export of food supplies, to enter into contractual transactions relating to the purchasing, storing, processing, selling and exporting of agricultural products, and in this connection to require any person to give information respecting his facilities for storing or processing of the same. These clauses contemplate a system of voluntary trading and appear to be clearly within the jurisdiction of parliament.
Clause 5, in effect, authorizes the minister, acting pursuant to regulations of the governor in council, to requisition supplies for the fulfilment of the contracts already referred to, and to determine the prices to be paid for such supplies. It is this power to requisition and fix prices that is called in question.
The decision of the privy council given in 1937, holding the Natural Products Marketing Act, 1934, to be invalid, has been mentioned as relevant to the question This act provided for the establishment of a dominion marketing board with power to regulate the time and place at which products should be marketed, and the manner of distribution, and the quantity and grade of the same, and to prohibit marketing of any products. It was held to be unconstitutional because, in effect, it purr
ported to regulate transactions completed within a province and having no connection with interprovincial or export trade; that is to say, the purpose of the act was to regulate the conduct of business including business confined to a single province.
The present bill has no such regulative purpose but is merely designed to enable the government to fulfil its international obligations to continue to sell and export food supplies to distressed countries in order to maintain economic stability and to insure an orderly transition from war to peace. These national obligations arise directly out of the war. The power to requisition supplies by the government for such a purpose would seem to me to be in no way analogous to the powers to regulate trading given by the Natural Products Marketing Act, 1934.
There is, however, to my mind, a very definite analogy between Bill 25 and the act of parliament relating to paper control enacted in 1919 and held by the Privy Council to be valid in the case of Fort Frances Pulp and Power Company Limited and Manitoba Free Press Company Limited. The purpose of that legislation was not only to control prices of paper but also to control the supply of paper itself during the abnormal conditions following the war of 1914-1918.
Reference is made in the preamble to the bill to an existing national emergency as establishing the need for the proposed legislation and it has been suggested that the validity of the statute depends on the existence^ of such a national emergency. In this connection the view has been put forward that as a result of the decision of the Privy Council in the recent case of Attorney General of Ontario et al v. Canada Temperance et al the existence of such an emergency is no longer a valid basis for an act of parliament which affects property and civil rights in the provinces. I do not read the Canada Temperance Act case as having this result but on the contrary it seems to me to be abundantly clear that it holds that an emergency may not be necessary to validate federal legislation which in another aspect touches upon matters specially reserved to the provincial legislatures. The true test, according to this decision, is whether the real subject matter of the act goes beyond local or provincial concern and must from its inherent nature be the concern of the dominion as a whole. Such an act is within the competence of parliament though it may in another aspect touch upon matters specially reserved to the provinces. I should think that Bill 25 satisfies this test.
In the most recent pronouncement upon the subject of the emergency legislative power of parliament, viz., in the Japanese reference, the privy council said that very clear evidence that an emergency has not arisen or that the emergency no longer exists is required to justify the judiciary in overruling the decision of the parliament of the dominion that exceptional measures were required and were still required.
For the reasons given it is my opinion that the bill is within the competence 'of parliament to enact.
I do not think it is necessary to add anything to that opinion. Yesterday the hon. member for Lake Centre put forward the view, not dogmatically but for the considera-
Agricultural Products Act

tion of the government-, that the doctrine of emergency no longer was valid as a basis for dominion jurisdiction. He cited in support of that position the Canada Temperance Act case, and stated that that position had been taken by the editor of the Fortnightly Law Journal, and perhaps by others. Bearing in mind what I said in reply to the hon. member for Temiscouata, I am not going to venture into an opinion on the matter. However, I have read the Canada Temperance Act case and the subsequent case, that of the Japanese reference, and it appears to me that the true effect of the decision in the Canada Temperance Act case is that there does not have to be an emergency to found jurisdiction on the part of the dominion; that the dominion may have the power even when there is no emergency to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada, even though its legislation touches upon matters ordinarily regarded as solely within provincial jurisdiction. In other words, the judgment of the judicial committee of the privy council as given by Lord Simon extends rather than narrows the powers of the dominion as they had therefore been conceived. It must be remembered- that the Canada Temperance Act decision was not against the dominion; it was in favour of the dominion. It held the Canada Temperance Act to be a valid exercise of dominion constitutional powers. I do not think that in any sense that judgment can be taken as a decision narrowing the powers of the dominion to legislate in a national emergency.
Even in that judgment it was said that an emergency may be the occasion of legislation which under the general powers of peace, order and good government is valid. The subsequent case, that of the Japanese reference, founded the powers of the dominion pretty solidly upon national emergency. If the hon. gentleman has read the headnote in the Dominion Law Reports report of the case he will see the vexation of the headnote writer at what he considered to be the inconsistency of the judicial committee of the privy council. But I do not think there is any real inconsistency there. In this case, the case of the Agricultural Products Marketing Act, if I were asked to describe the nature of the emergency referred to in the preamble, I would describe it, perhaps not in legal or court language but in practical language, as being something like this: Great national interests are at stake in the sense that as an aftermath of the war the economic stability of the greatest national

customer that this country has had in the past is endangered and it is in the national interest that food should continue to flow to the people of Great Britain in order that they may be in a position to produce goods and exchange them for our goods in the future and continue to be the great market that they have been in the past.
If a condition arises under which that position is imperilled as a result of war and during the war and for a reasonable time after the war, there is an emergent and extraordinary situation which puts in danger great national interests and justifies legislation by this parliament under the heading of peace, order and good government. As I say, these may not be the only aspects of the emergency but these aspects are, I submit, sufficient to occasion a valid exercise of the powers under the peace, order and good government clause.
To sum up:	We do not need, under the
Canada Temperance Act case, to establish a national emergency. Under that case a national emergency may be the occasion for passing legislation which is valid under the peace, order and good government clause. If there is a national emergency, that in itself may be the foundation of our jurisdiction, under the Japanese reference case and under the Fort Frances case. The emergent or extraordinary circumstances in this post-war situation, are, I believe, sufficient to form the basis of a valid exercise of the dominion's constitutional powers in the manner set out in the bill before the house. In that opinion I am supported by the Deputy Minister of Justice.

I thank my right
hon. friend for the detail in which he has answered the question I raised yesterday as to the constitutionality of this measure and of others that are before the house whose constitutionality must be dependent upon grounds other than that they come exclusively within the powers of the dominion parliament. I am not entering into any argument with the minister on this question because, as the minister said, no one can be dogmatic on matters such as this. After all it is not what one's opinion may be that ultimately determines the question; the final determinant will be the courts of the land. Equally strong opinions were given in 1934 as to the constitutionality of the Natural Products Marketing Act and the other measures of reform legislation which were so necessary to the welfare of the people but which, by reason of the distribution of powers as between

Agricultural Products Act
the dominion and the provinces the courts determined were not within the legislative ambit of the dominion parliament.
I shall do no more than place before the committee the supporting evidence to which I made reference yesterday. I referred to Mr. Chitty, K.C. and his opinion given in the Fortnightly Law Journal of June 1, 1946, shortly after the opinion of the privy council had been handed down. Without going into detail, the conclusion to which he came was that the privy council had exploded the emergency doctrine.
As I listened to the minister today I was impressed by this fact, that there must be a line of demarcation when the federal parliament may no longer contend that the powers are exercised not because they come under section	91 but	being	under section	92	areavailable because they arise under the peace, order and good government clause. As I understood the minister's justification of this legislation it was that the economic stability of the	United	Kingdom, our	greatest	customer,	was in	grave	danger;	that	it	was
necessary in the interests of our own ecoriomic survival to preserve that economic unit, and for that reason the dominion must be presumed to have the power to entrench upon property and civil rights within the provinces. The arguments of those holding that view were dealt with in this article by Mr. Chitty in these words:
Much therefore as our constitutional theorist friends	would like to	see the	Fort	Frances
case-
To which the Minister of Justice made reference:
[DOT]-as a precedent for an all-powerful dominion that could create emergencies at its whim and arrogate to itself overriding powers to legislate in any sphere without regard to the views of the provinces, we are afraid that even the Fort Frances case is a broken reed. That case never went further, as a sound precedent, than to decide that the emergency upon the existence of which the right to resort to government by order in council under the War Measures Act depended might continue to exist even after the war had officially come to an end.
The great danger with legislation such as this, commendable as it may be, is that a government may centralize power in Ottawa to the detriment of the provinces under the excuse of an emergency by the simple expedient by setting forth in the preamble that an emergency exists. There is danger to the set-up of confere elation in emergency legislation or in legislation passed under the general powers relating to peace, order and good government; for surely there must come some point where
the dominion cannot use such an excuse of an emergency to secure for itself the power to interfere with the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces over property and civil rights.
More than that I am not going to say. I have raised the point and the law officers have given their opinion. But in regard to this legislation and also the wheat board legislation which requires compulsory powers it is interesting to note that away back in 1922 an opinion was given by the then deputy minister of justice denying the right of parliament to pass legislation compulsorily controlling the distribution or sale of farm products.

In 1921, and the question arose as to the continuance of the wheat board that was in existence during the first world war and in particular as to the power of the dominion parliament to pass legislation compulsorily dealing with wheat. The then prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, at page 940 of Hansard of April 19, 1922, read the opinion of Mr. Newcombe, an outstanding lawyer, then deputy minister of justice, and subsequently a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada. I am not going to read it in detail. The Prime Minister on that occasion said this:
With reference to the fourth report of the select standing committee on agriculture and colonization, in which the house concurred on the eleventh instant, I may say that the government has obtained the written opinion of the law officers of the crown upon the question thereby suggested as to the constitutionality of the reconstruction of the Canadian wheat board, and that opinion is now submitted for the information of the house.
There were many who believed that the Canadian wheat board should be continued, but it was discontinued in 1921. The Prime Minister at that time gave the opinion of the law officers of the crown, and this is the essence of that opinion. It will be found at page 942 of Hansard of 1922:
It is Clear that so long as a subject matter of legislation finds place within the enumerations of provincial powers it does not belong to the dominion under its general authority to make laws for the peace, order and good government
Agricultural Products Act

of Canada. It ia certain that the essential compulsory powers of the wheat board are prima facie included in the provincial enumeration of property and civil rights or local matters in the provinces. In my opinion these powers do not lie within the field which may be occupied by the execution of the dominion power to regulate trade and commerce, as that power has been expounded in successive decisions by the ultimate tribunal of appeal; and I think it may be affirmed without uncertainty that the necessary reconstructive powers are not comprehended in any other of the dominion enumerations. While I do not suggest a doubt that conditions of export from the dominion and foreign trade relations may be regulated by parliament, I am impressed with the view that these powers cannot be made a cover for legislation which denies the freedom of contract, capacity to buy and sell and the maintenance and exercise of proprietary rights which exist under the provincial laws. The powers of criminal legislation which belong exclusively to the dominion are in their application to this case of an ancillary character and cannot as such be invoked to afford a sanction for measures in themselves ultra vires. Consequently it is my opinion that the reconstruction of the wheat board in the present circumstances with the powers conferred thereon by the orders in council is a project constitutionally incompetent to the parliament of Canada.
The opinion of the then deputy minister of justice, Mr Newcombe, was concurred in by the minister of justice, Sir Lomer Gouin, and by Mr. D. D. McKenzie, who was leader of the Liberal party in 1917 and until the present Prime Minister became the leader. The essence of the opinion was that the compulsory features that were part and parcel of the Wheat Board Act were ultra vires. You will remember, sir, that after the first great war there was a serious economic condition. We have heard it repeated on a number of occasions in this chamber that prices were up and that subsequently there was deflation. These deflationary conditions were to a large extent in existence in 1921 and continued in 1922; yet at that time, even though it would have been of great benefit to the farmers to have the wheat board continued-and the western farmers demanded the continuation of the wheat board because of the then existing economic conditions-the opinion of the Department of Justice was that the granting of compulsory powers to control the direction, the diversion or distribution of wheat was not within the power of parliament.
I present this argument, sir, for the purpose of placing before the committee the other side of the question and the opinions given by another deputy minister of justice during a time of serious economic emergency.
I want to thank the minister for the opinion he has given. I have discharged my responsibility in asking for it.

I should like to make a suggestion to the minister on this section. As has been pointed out by various ministers, this is to fulfil contracts with Britain, and one of the most important items cited has been the bacon contracts with Britain, in which we have fallen short in the last few years. Coupled with this matter, the minister on March 17 made an announcement as to prices to be paid for oats and barley for the feeding of animals for meat products for those contracts, setting a floor price of 90 cents for barley, and pointing out that there would be a drawback or payment of 25 cents a bushel for that barley to those who did not grow barley and feed animals; and coupled with that, that there' would be free freight from Fort William to eastern points and from Calgary and Edmonton to the west. That means that the people who produce the grain are certainly not going to feed hogs in the prairie provinces. It gets away entirely from the theory that we have always been led to believe in, that industry should be established close or adjacent to raw materials and power.
I do not think anyone will deny that if we are to have a sound economic system there is some truth in that theory, and therefore much the soundest economy would be to feed the animals on the same farm where the feed is grown for them. It would avoid dislocation in man-power and get rid of transportation difficulties.

speechtext:
I should like to discuss first the power of requisition. With deference to the minister and to your previous ruling, Mr. Chairman, it is difficult to discuss the power under this section because it gives only the authority to make regulations for carrying out the power already conferred. It is merely specified here, so that there will be no question that that power exists and that regulations may be made for the purpose of enforcing that power. It would have been more appropriate to discuss it earlier, and that is why I am under some difficulty in discussing it now.
In view of the fact that the minister has said that he would not oppose latitude of discussion on this section, perhaps I can put forward the views I have. What I wish to ask is whether the minister would be willing to accept an amendment which would limit his powers to requisition. The effort which has been made by the official opposition in regard 83166-100i
to this bill was mainly to get a complete marketing act, so that there would be no question that the producers who are affected would have a say as to the quantities and the prices of commodities mentioned in these international agreements, and the regulations and terms upon which they were marketed and exported. If that had been done, then the objection that I am about to make would no longer apply. Since that has not been done, we are in the position where the minister alone sets the prices under an international agreement and indicates the quantity which shall be delivered.
We have been able to get only a limited assurance that he must discuss the matter with the producers boards before he does that. Therefore we are in the position, as was established, I think, with some degree of conclusiveness in the wheat agreement and the position which seems to prevail in the cheese and egg agreement, where the producers feel that their produce is being sold at a price which hardly pays them the cost of production. That is adopted as a matter of government policy in order to assist in the reconstruction of Great Britain particularly and of the continent of Europe. With that policy there is no disagreement, but with the administration of the policy there is a large degree of disagreement because we feel that the farmer should not be expected to bear the burden of the policy alone.
Briefly to recapitulate, we feel that if the farmer through his producer boards were able to set the price and the quantity there would be no danger of his having to bear the burden of what might be a disadvantageous agreement. Since that is not the case the minister can make further contracts which may be bad ones from the point of view of business and which may involve the farmer in heavy financial losses when compared with what he might be obtaining were his produce not being sold exclusively subject to the terms of the agreement. The position is this:	if the minister,
since he is now in exclusive charge of making these contracts, sets the prices, he may make a food agreement, and he can then step in and requisition all the agricultural produce he needs in order to fulfil the agreement. If he did not have the power of requisitioning, the only way he could fulfil his agreement would be by buying on the market at the current price which presumably, under normal circumstances would be a price which would repay the farmer his cost of production and give him some profit. Therefore I wish to suggest, first, that by taking this power to requisition everything the minister is in a 
Agricultural Products Act

position where he may be able to enforce the terms of a bad agreement and make the farmer bear the whole of the burden instead of distributing it across the country. The minister has said that in some instances it is necessary to have the power to requisition, and he referred specifically to bacon. It is agreed that if we make contracts the minister must have reasonable power to carry them out. I do not think anyone would question that; but we should like to preserve this principle, that the cost of carrying it out must be borne by the country as a whole and not by the agricultural producer alone. I ask specifically whether the minister will limit his power to requisition to that necessary to fulfil the bacon agreement? At the moment I cannot conceive of any other agreement where he needs the power to requisition and where the circumstances would be the same as that which affects the bacon agreement.
As I say, the only time he would need the power to requisition is where he sold large quantities of produce at a low price which would make the farmers unwilling to part with their produce, which would necessitate his stepping in and requisitioning.
Although we may have the assurance of the minister that it is not intended to make bad agreements and then step in and requisition to enforce these agreements, I do not think it is a proper principle for the house, and for the opposition in particular, to accept this assurance, for the reasons which were put forward by the Minister of Justice in the argument which he made in 1934 and to which I have referred. He did not think it was proper for parliament to grant powers the exercise of which it did not approve. That is the position in which we find ourselves at the present time.
Just today I came across an argument used on March 3 in the British House of Commons, which puts the position so clearly that I should like to read it. I put this argument forward to the minister in all sincerity; I am not even suggesting specific amendment myself; but I am asking him if he will, to meet these views, see fit to find a way of limiting his powers of requisition so that they cover only the bacon contracts. The particular thought I have in mind in making this suggestion was used in an argument by Sir Arthur Salter in the British House of Commons on March 3, when he referred to a number of bills which, he maintained, granted excessive power. In these bills, he said:
. . . clauses have been drafted so widely, that it has been easy for us to demonstrate that quite fantastic abusive action could be taken
IMr. Fulton.l
within the powers of the bill. When this has been demonstrated, the minister has always said:	"That is not what I intend to do. I
intend to do so and so. I have quite a reasonable policy." We may agree that the minister is sincere and that his policy is reasonable, but we cannot properly accept such assurances as alternatives to drafting the law in such a way as to define his powers. Otherwise, we abdicate from our position as legislators. We are concerned in this house, as legislators, with the legal intention which is to be inferred from the words of a bill, and not with ministerial intentions or assurances which do not bind even their successors of the same government and still less their successors in another government, while the measure itself, with all the powers which were given originally, still survives.
That is exactly the feeling I have with regard to this bill and particularly sections 3 and 5, which give the minister complete power to walk on to every farm in Canada and requisition such produce at such prices as he wishes. I am quite certain that he himself will agree that he does not intend to exercise that power and that he does not need to have all that power for carrying into effect the agreements he has made, and which he may contemplate making. I put these views before him and before the house, coupled with a request that he himself introduce an amendment imposing upon his power of requisition such limitations as will confine it to those things which he absolutely must do in order to carry out the specific agreements he has in mind.

On the last suggestion, I would say that the intention of this bill is not to give us authority to interfere in interprovincial trade in a manner which I think is suggested here. We have arrangements with Britain, under which we send certain fruits to that country. We go into different provinces and arrange for the purchase of it. That, to my mind, has much the same effect as the hon. member for Yale has in mind. If there are berries in British Columbia that are in surplus and they are not able to handle them,
we have during the war been making arrangements to take such surpluses and ship them to Britain. We make that arrangement with the British government. That has met all difficulties and, I think, will meet all difficulties, as long as the situation created by this act exists. I understand that what the hon. member has in mind is that when this situation does not exist there may develop something similar to what we had before the war, the difficulty in interprovincial trade. But this was not intended to take care of that situation, but to meet the situation in relation to apples. There are producers' organizations across the country and they are in a position to enter into interprovincial arrangements. There is nothing particularly legal about it, in the sense that the suggested organization in Ontario is not legalized under provincial statute in the same way as some of the others may be.

speechtext: Does the provincial statute give the board power to deal interprovincially without corresponding legislation here?

They are able to come to understandings, and if by those understandings they are able to carry out an agreement that we may make with Britain, they have come to us and asked us to try to make that agreement. They said that, in order to guarantee carrying it out, we would require to exercise some authority in connection with interprovincial trade in apples. Under those circumstances we go to the British and say maybe we can make some adjustment that will be satisfactory to both of us, probably our people could use more of some other

commodity. The suggestion has been made that we took too much cheese from this market. We can go to the British and say, "It will suit our people much better if we leave cheese on this market, or a considerable part of it, and we should like you to take apples." Things of that kind can be negotiated by the government, which would not be understood as between individual organizations in Canada. The apple producers would not feel like talking against the cheese producer, or the British would not pay any attention to them if they did. But when the government goes to the British and says that it would suit Canada better if you take our surplus apples, our people will eat cheese up to a certain level, then we can get an arrangement made with them. That is the kind of thing we will be doing. On the apples, we hope to sell this fifty per cent or whatever it is they generally trade in with Britain, to the British. We are not concerned about who makes the deal, as long as it can be made. But the apple growers wish us to have the authority to make it, and that is what this gives.
On the other question of requisitioning, I am afraid that I cannot say very much more than the government said in Great Britain. I would presume that they obtained their authority from the House of Commons in Great Britain or from the parliament in Great Britain.

speechtext:
It is exactly the same principle, and I think it applies to almost every piece of legislation we pass in this house about giving greater authority to somebody, than that somebody, whoever it is, ever hopes that he will have to use. He uses it only in very extreme cases.
In relation to these contracts, the only kind of circumstances under which we would use requisitioning is this. We are the lowest per capita cheese eaters in any country in the world for which any records are kept. We eat fewer pounds per head of population than any other country. The British are the largest per capita cheese eaters in the world. According to the last records I saw, they ate sixteen pounds per head of population prior to the war. We ate three. On top of that the market for sixty per cent of our cheese prior to the war was in Britain, and it has been during the war.
It has been my experience that the cheese producers themselves have agreed to our taking cheese and sending it to Great Britain as a part of the policy that was being followed of attempting to help feed Britain with the kind of food they could best get from Canada during
fMr. Gardiner.]
the period. We would not take the suggested action. I am sure our friends opposite would give us credit for having more political sense than to take cheese off the market in Canada, and send it over to Britain at a lower price than could be obtained for it in Canada, just to carry out an agreement. We would not do it for that purpose at all.
On the general question of requisitioning to do a thing like that, we would deal with the cheese boards in Canada and find out their attitude. We would discuss the matter with them. We could not carry it out without their cooperation, because cheese will keep over a very long period of time if you put it away in the proper storage, and you must keep it for ninety days. So these people could put their cheese away and keep it if we did not have that cooperation. But they cooperated with us 100 per cent, because we discussed our intentions with them and had their agreement before acting. The reason why they want us to act is that ninety per cent of them say, "It should be done," and there is no hesitation about it. But there is another small percentage who will not cooperate unless compelled. The. others say, "We should like to do this and will if you say that they should do it." - It is really the same principle as that contained in the legislation which my hon. friends voted for the other night, that the producer should be in a position to sav to the minority, "under the circumstances, you must do this."

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext: You are following that practice.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
We are following that practice, and I admit it quite frankly, in this bill. We have been doing it over a period during the war and we are still doing it.
Let us consider the packers. After all, there is not a great deal of difference in human nature whether it is packers, farmers or others. Some forty packers have inspected plants and we must get all our bacon and ham from those plants. Suppose the forty of them are absolutely agreed to do the thing which is required to be done. They have sat in and discussed it. Everybody has discussed it. The advisers we have from the farm organizations have discussed it, and we have sometimes brought them together and had it discussed. Then they say, "All right, that is the thing to be done. Let us go ahead and do it." Two weeks after we get doing that, there are two packing plants somewhere who say, "I am not going to do that. I can make more money doing something else." The others wish us to have the authority to say to those fellows, "Well, the government can really requisition your product." Up to date I do not think we have

Agricultural Products Act
had to do much requisitioning under it. We just simply make the suggestion. An inspector goes out, looks over the situation and says "Well, we have the authority to compel you to do it, and the other companies are all doing it. Why don't you do it?" That is about all that ever happens. But if we did not have the authority there is the very small percentage of those with whom we are dealing who would just say, "You do what you like; I am going to do as I like." That is the principle which is behind the requisitioning.
There is no intention of going out and grabbing off large amounts in order to try to fill contracts. It may be thought that these contracts have not been good ones, but every time they have been made we have sat down wfith the British; and if it is a bacon contract, we have sat dowm with the packers. We have sent out the best investigators we could find to ascertain how many hogs were going to be produced within the year. Then we have made the best investigations possible to find out how much will be consumed in Canada. We balance it all up and say what we can do. Last year we said, "We can give you only 267,000,000 pounds of bacon and ham." Prior to that we.had been giving as much as 700,000,000 pounds, but last year we said that we could give only 267,000,000 pounds. We hope to reach levels after we have stated them, and we have to do a little of what is called requisitioning in order to get up to that reasonable level. But we are intending to do what was suggested in this case. We have no intention of utilizing it to do any unreasonable thing. I do not think the house would expect that even a Liberal government would intentionally be so foolish. We do want to do the things which are reasonable. We want to have the power to do reasonable things, and nothing more than that. But we must have the power if we are to be able to take limited amounts here and there, or go into a plant and say, "So far as your production is concerned, a certain percentage ought to go to the British contract." But as far as going out and saying that we will take it wholesale, that is not the intention.

Section 7 is another illustration of something that we have met several times during this session which, to my mind,

Agricultural Products Act
is a definite attempt, or, if not an attempt, an indication of the government's continuing to employ people working for the government or for corporations or commissions of the government without reference to the Civil Service Act. I believe that that is an ignoring of one of the greatest supports and safeguards we have for the public servants of this dominion. Here we have a board set up with power to use their absolute discretion to hire, fire or employ those whom they wish under such terms as they like, irrespective of the services or the Civil Service Act.
The Civil Service Act as it now stands gives a great deal of protection to those loyal people in Canada who have worked for the government and have given brilliant service. There are privileges connected with it; they know their rights; they know their tenure of office is governed by an act of parliament. They know they are not subject to the whim or fancy of some individual employee on a temporary day-to-day basis with personal likes and dislikes interfering with the natural employment of the civil servant.
I can see no reason whatever why employees, clerks and many professional, technical and other officers should be hired by this board in a different way from permanent civil servants. I see no reason why this board should want so to hire them. If one reads the Gordon report on civil service matters he will find that that commission has within the confines of its directives recommended certain improvements in the Civil Service Act. One of the most important of those recommendations suggested a more expeditious and more efficient way of employing highly trained technical and professional men. This bill goes a long way beyond that.
The Gordon report recommended that the Civil Service Act should, in effect, be the procurement branch for those people whom the government wants to employ. This bill ignores that. As I understand it, the Gordon report recommended that the civil service commission ought to be the employment agency for those men whose services are sought by government, boards or commissions, I cannot see why the government wants to ignore the operation of the Civil Service Act, wants to put it in the limbo of forgotten memories rather than use it and improve it.
If these boards cannot get satisfactory employees through the civil service commission, why do the government not say, we do not want the Civil Service Act? Why do they try to make as many employment agencies as they possibly can, outside the confines of the Civil Service Act? It does interfere with our public service. As I have said before, hon.
members should bear in mind that we cannot very well hire three or four different sets of employees without having them compare each other, without having some jealousy, bitterness and antagonism arise with respect to the rights and privileges granted each one. I think we are introducing a dangerous doctrine by having the government bring before us a bill setting up boards, commissions and crown companies and having the employees of these bodies removed from governmental responsibility and from parliament itself. It amounts to a dictatorial privilege of hiring, firing, employing and granting privileges beyond the Civil Service Act. The civil servants of Canada have had a long tradition of rights and privileges and of stability of employment. They know what they get under the Civil Service Act. I do not know what they will get under this bill or what their term of employment will be. Many factors enter into the matter, and I think the minister might very well give it further consideration, particularly in relation to officers, employees and clerks. There may be some excuse for having highly trained, technical men put on some special ground, because they are few in number and are specialists in their field, but there is no excuse for having ordinary employees and clerks, with no better qualifications, no different abilities, and in no different situations, hired by a board of this kind on a basis different from that on which the permanent civil service operates. Would the minister not take that suggestion into consideration and allow the section to stand until he sees whether he can bring in a provision that will have all these people within the scope of the Civil Service Act?

The members of the boards are practically all civil servants, though there are a few' taken in from outside, such as those mentioned in connection with the meat board the other day. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I rise to a question of privilege. I have received from you a cable regarding a statement I made in this house on Monday evening concerning Sir Waldron Smithers, M.P. The cable reads: Speaker,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
Please tell William Bryce his criticism of me due to misunderstanding. Hansard reports when I was there in Canada dollar wheat showed good profit to consumer. That was thirty-five years ago. Please ask Bryce give equal publicity. Respectful good wishes.
Waldron Smithers,
Commons, London.
If Sir Waldron Smithers had been well enough informed about Canadian affairs to be justified in making any statement as to what would constitute a fair price for wheat, he should know as much about conditions in Canada today as we know about conditions in Britain. If he had possessed that knowledge he never would have made the statement which he was reported to have made, and which his cable appears to confirm. I still think the knight owes this country an apology for a statement which is the reverse of the fact.
Let me repeat this statement again: If we had done what he alleges we did, we would have demanded the market price, at least for the wheat, and that would be around S3 a bushel instead of the $1.55 Britain pays today. And let me say, I do not begrudge this bargain to Britain because it affords an opportunity for us to assist Britain in her present difficulties, which we are proud and glad to do. In the second place, it lays a base for the establishment of stabilized prices for our products. I personally, along with many Canadian farmers, resent being insulted by one who is a beneficiary of our favourable agreement.

speechtext:
Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for

Emergency Powers
a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war and to provide therein that the governor in council may appoint and fix the compensation of the officers, clerks and employees necessary for the administration of any order or regulation continued in force by the act and further to provide that certain officers, clerks and employees may continue to perform the duties for which they were previously appointed.
He said:	The object of the bill which will
be based upon this resolution is to continue in force for a period not exceeding one year from March 31 next a specified group of orders and regulations of the governor in council which were passed under the War Measures Act or the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945. In the speech from the throne Ilis Excellency stated the intention of the government in the following terms:
The policy of the government is to maintain only such price and commodity controls as may be required to protect consumers from a sudden and drastic rise in the cost of living, and to ensure the fair distribution of essential goods and services which are in short supply. You will be invited to consider what measures may be necessary to continue this policy after the expiry of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act. Where it may appear advisable to continue these or other transitional measures, the required legislation will be submitted for your approval at the earliest possible date.
The proposed bill will set forth all the measures of an emergency nature which the government considers it is necessary or expedient to retain subsequent to the expiry of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945. The government does not recommend that parliament confer upon the governor in council any general powers to make orders and regulations with respect to general subject matters. Rather it is considered that the stage in progress of this country from war to peace has been reached where it is possible to carry out the policies of translation and decontrol upon the basis of powers which are contained in orders and regulations of the governor in council now in existence.
Hon. members will recall that upon the outbreak of the war in 1939 the War Measures Act came into force upon a proclamation of the governor in council declaring that a state of war existed. That statute conferred upon the governor in council the widest possible powers. Only the extreme nature of the emergency with which the country was faced justified the vesting of such powers in the executive, but this crisis made it imperative that wide powers should be exercisable in a speedy and flexible manner.
With the cessation of hostilities in 1945 it became apparent that, while the emergency created by the war had not by any means come to an end, the extensive powers necessary to meet the day to day exigencies involved in the active prosecution of the war were no longer necessary. Parliament was accordingly advised that the situation no longer called for the continued use of the powers conferred by the War Measures Act, but that powers of a less extensive nature would be sufficient. Parliament accordingly, being of the opinion that the national emergency arising out of the war continued to exist, conferred upon the governor in council power to make regulations for the purpose of (a) providing for and maintaining the armed forces of Canada during the occupation of enemy territory and demobilization and providing for the rehabilitation of members thereof; (b) facilitating the readjustment of industry and commerce to the requirements of the community in time of peace; (c) maintaining, controlling and regulating supplies and services, prices, transportation, use and occupation of property, rentals, employment, salaries and wages to ensure economic stability and an orderly transition to conditions of peace; (d) assisting the relief of suffering and the restoration and distribution of essential supplies and services in any part of His Majesty's dominions or in foreign countries that are in grave distress as the result of the war, or (e) continuing or discontinuing in an orderly manner, as the emergency permits, measures adopted during and by reason of the war.
The National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, as amended by chapter 60 of the statutes of 1946, expires on March 29 next. The government, however, must advise the house that the national emergency arising out of the war cannot yet be said to have come to an end and that the time has not yet come when emergency measures can be wholly discontinued. In particular, let me emphasize that the time is not appropriate for the complete removal of emergency economic controls for reasons which I shall give later. The government, therefore, while prepared to recommend that the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act be allowed to expire according to its terms, is nevertheless of opinion that certain transitional measures should be continued for the time being.
These measures, of which office consolidations have been printed and circulated to hon. members of the house, fall into three classes which may be described in very general terms as regulative, administrative and legislative. Examples of regulative orders are those auth-
Emergency Powers

orizing the continuance of price control, rent control, eviction control, the control of distribution and supply, including rationing. Examples of administrative orders are those relating to members and former members of the armed forces and merchant seamen, the disposition of claims against the crown arising overseas out of the war and the administration of property of the Japanese in Canada. The orders which I have called legislative are the orders relating to old age pensions, veterans preference in the civil service and labour relations. The reason I put those in a special category is that they will be replaced later this session by acts of parliament.
As the house was informed last August, a committee of officers of the Department of Justice and the other departments concerned under the direction of the Solicitor General has since the latter part of 1945 kept under continuous examination and review the orders in council passed as emergency measures. Recommendations for revocation of orders have been made from time to time, and the committee has reported that all but the measures appearing in the office consolidations to which I referred can be allowed to expire with the expiry of (he National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945.
However I should state that there will be a supplement to the office consolidations which will be distributed and which will contain two other orders relating to the control of atomic energy. For reasons which have appeared since the office consolidations were printed, it has appeared that these are orders which it is believed should be continued under the authority of this legislation.

[Mr. Ilsley.l
As I said earlier in my remarks, the time is not appropriate for the complete removal of these important emergency economic controls. While much progress has been made in expanding our peacetime production, and while the flow of output is gathering increasing momentum, production in a number of important fields has not yet overtaken the high level of demand which in some cases, like that of housing, has been accumulating for years.
Moreover, the consequences of the war are still very apparent in external markets. Worldwide shortages of basic materials and foodstuffs limit the supplies of a number of goods available in Canada. On the one hand, they mean extraordinarily large and urgent demands for Canadian foodstuffs, raw materials and other goods, and on the other hand, they limit the supplies of such imported1 basic commodities as sugar, vegetable oils, tin and steel. High and fluctuating prices in world markets give us some idea of the sort of market conditions which would be reflected in Canada if all controls, including export controls, were dropped at this time. While the government has been moving as promptly as conditions warranted in removing controls, there can be little doubt that an immediate removal of all remaining controls would have very serious and undesirable consequences.
In some cases, the consequences are quite obvious. For example, I do not think there can be much question as to what would happen if the controls over rentals and evictions were removed in present circumstances. In the face of the continuing shortage of housing accommodation, it is clear enough that rents would rise sharply and that evictions would be counted in the tens of thousands.
Some hon. MEMBEBS: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Absolutely true; and anyone wrho denies it is just living apart from the facts.
The results of a sudden removal of price and other controls over such commodities as sugar and vegetable oils, where external prices are high and supplies difficult to obtain, must be equally apparent. Prices would not only rise sharply, but distribution would be uneven and disorderly, and the needs of many citizens could not be met. In the face of the international conditions in the economic sphere and of the gaps which, though narrowing, still persist between domestic supplies and demands, there can be no doubt that prices of foods, textiles, fuels and, of course, rentals would rise suddenly and substantially. The same thing would be true of many basic materials, with consequent additional pressure on the

Emergency Powers
prices of many manufactured goods. And not only would prices and living costs advance suddenly and sharply, but we would also be plunged into a condition of disorderly markets, and perhaps soon after would be faced with widespread price declines with their inevitable restrictive effects on production and employment.
I do not suggest that we would be faced with uncontrollable inflation on the central European or Chinese pattern. That obviously is not the case. Production in this country has increased too much for that sort of thing, and we did not, during the war, suffer disorganization and destruction in our domestic economy.
I do say, however, that we would have a sudden and marked increase in our price level, and in the cost of living, which would rapidly carry us toward the notably higher level of prices prevailing in the United States.
One can readily imagine how an abrupt and substantial rise in living costs would contribute to an unsettled state of industrial relations and to delays and interruptions in the production of goods which are so eagerly demanded. It is not difficult to appreciate the hardship and the reduction in living standards that would result for the many families whose incomes are relatively fixed-wage-earners, school teachers, white-collar workers, pensioners and so on. That there would be profiteering and speculation in the necessities of life can be taken for granted. And it is an absolute certainty that many prices, after rising suddenly, would fluctuate widely, and later on decline perhaps as abruptly as they went up. To remove all controls now would be to ask for a sudden and disruptive jump in our prices and living costs at the very time when we can begin to see ahead of us the completion of the job of orderly readjustment. We would be throwing away many of the advantages of the policy which Canada has successfully followed when, with a little more persistence and a little more patience we could pilot ourselves through the difficult period of readjustment without the dislocation and economic disorder which usually follows war.
If we are to achieve an orderly readjustment it will be necessary to continue a number of controls for the time being. I cannot subscribe in any way to the opinion that immediate decontrol would be more conducive to more orderly conditions than the policy of gradual and planned decontrol which the government is following. We have before us the experience of the United States where all
price controls except those over rents and two specified commodities were removed not long ago.

speechtext:
That experience gives a very fair idea of what could have been expected in this country had we followed a similar course. What did happen in the United States can be described in its broad outlines quite briefly. In the seven months following June 30, 1948, when O.P.A.'s powers first expired, the official cost of living index rose 20 points, from 33 per cent over the pre-war level to 53 per cent over that level. The food component of the cost of living index rose by 38 points during the same seven months. The general level of wholesale prices in the United States, which was 40 per cent over the prewar level in June, 1946, was 76 per cent over that level in January 1947, and has not declined since.
Not only have prices risen sharply in the United States, but those of a number of important commodities have fluctuated widely and in a manner which it would be very difficult to describe as orderly. To take two very important examples, prices of beef and pork in the United States have been showing remarkable gyrations. The wholesale price of beef in New York jumped from its former ceiling at the end of June of somewhat over $20 per hundredweight, to S55 early in July. It then came down to around 836 and a ceiling of around S25 was reimposed in September. When that ceiling came off the price soared to $62 and then it fell again and the latest quotation is around $40. We can see the same sort of story in pork, in lard and in butter. Whatever else it may be, it is not a picture of orderly conditions. There are, of course, many other prices that have gone up and have not come down. The prices of cotton fabrics rose in line with the rise in the price of raw cotton which was not under price control until the time when controls over textile prices were dropped. Since then the price of raw cotton has shown some decline, but the prices of fabrics have risen very substantially. While no one would suggest that Canadian consumers like the price increase that it has been necessary to authorize in this country, it must surely be clear that the immediate removal of the economic purchasing controls would involve much greater price increases, widely fluctuating markets and opportunities for speculation and exploitation which ought to be apparent to anyone who takes the trouble to examine the actual background of our present position.

The system which we have had to date has worked and the administration has been efficient and reasonable. Though there are some people who have made quite unjustified insinuations about the wartime bureaucrats, the record of the prices board in efficiency, fairness, and honest administration speaks for itself.
