Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) has suggested that the main debate on this matter take place on the second reading of the bill which will later be introduced rather than that we debate it at this time. With that suggestion we in this party are in entire agreement.
I wish to take but a moment now to outline the position as I see it. The motion before us is to go into committee of the whole to consider the expedience of introducing a measure providing for the temporary extension of certain transitional measures beyond March 29, measures which would ordinarily terminate at that time unless provision is now made for extending them.

The proposed bill, from the statements made by the minister at an earlier time, will deal with about fifty-five different orders in council. The main principle is the extension of the powers granted in all these orders in council. But these orders in council are of varying degrees of importance and they differ widely from one another. I think the idea now of going into committee of the whole, where we may ask the minister questions and then, later on, debate the main principles in the bill, is a good suggestion.
Speaking for this party, I may say we are agreeable to passing this motion at this stage, asking for certain further information in committee, and then, with the bill before us, and at a later time, as the minister suggests, going ahead with the debate.
We propose to reserve the right either to support or to oppose the different sections of the bill in committee of the whole, and to debate the whole general question on second reading. Under those circumstances we are agreeable to the passage of this motion at this time.
Mr. M. J. COLDWELL (Rosetown-Biggar) [DOT] Usually when a suggestion of this kind is made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) or any other minister of the government we try to fall in line with it, but on this occasion I think one must say something more than a few cursory words regarding the motion now before us. I say this, Mr. Speaker, because, as will be seen from the remarks I shall make, we wish to place ourselves on record regarding the whole policy of controls and the policy of the government in regard to decontrols.
If it were necessary tonight to make out a case against decontrols to a greater extent than I am inclined to make it just now, I think that has been done in large measure by the minister himself. His defence of the controls that have been in effect, his statement regarding the situation which developed in the great country to the south last July and again last October, is, I think, a sufficient vindication of the main controls that have been put into effect in Canada and a vindication of those of us who believe that, instead of entering upon a policy of rapid decontrol, even on a planned basis, we should, in the interests of the Canadian people, not only maintain useful controls but, in some instances, even reimpose controls that have been lifted.
The resolution to be considered precedes the introduction of a measure-what for?- to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations for a limited period

Emergency Powers
during the national emergency arising out of the war; in short, by an act of this parliament to authorize the continuance of certain controls for a certain limited but unspecified period. I wish to say on behalf of this party that we shall seek to amend this motion in order to provide for consideration by the government and by this house of a different policy, the policy of maintaining beneficial controls and indeed, where necessary, of instituting comprehensive controls in order to protect the interests of the Canadian people.
I know perfectly well that in doing this we run counter to a great deal of propaganda in this country, propaganda that has gone on ever since, before the war ended. The amazing thing about this propaganda is that, while it has had some effect in, shall I say, political circles, it has had hardly any effect upon the general public. The recent Gallup polls indicate that conclusively. In the Gallup poll of Canadian public opinion, published in a number of Canadian newspapers on January 18 of this year, sixty-six per cent, or two-thirds of the persons interviewed at that time, answered "no" to the following question:	"There has
been talk of taking price controls off everything but rents after Christmas. Would you approve?" Sixty-six per cent answered, "no"; only twenty-seven per cent answered, "yes", and the remaining seven per cent apparently had no opinion to express. Since then, a number of labour and agricultural conferences have taken place: the United Farmers of Alberta, affiliates of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in various places, the Canadian Congress of Labour and other organizations. All of them, by resolution, have urged the maintenance of controls in the interests of the Canadian producer and of the Canadian consumer.
Last night I listened to an interesting and, I may add, an excellent radio address by the hon. gentleman who is parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) (Mr. Mayhew). But the tenor of that address was how beneficial the controls which had been instituted and maintained had been for the Canadian people. The minister himself tonight made a somewhat similar case on behalf of the controls. Yet controls are being discontinued, even while this parliament sits, I think in the face of public opinion in this country.
The voice of the executive council of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, heard from the city of Toronto on January 28, and demanding the removal of controls as soon as possible, has been, more effective, I believe and heard more distinctly, shall I put it, in

this chamber than the voices of the masses of the Canadian people. What is forgotten is that the demand from private interests is a demand for the ending of public controls instituted in the public interest, for the ending of public controls now under the authority of this parliament, that is, by authority of the elected representatives of the people. I say to this house that the question we should be considering is a different one. We should be concerned, not with the elimination of controls by public bodies, but with the elimination of controls by private corporations, the elimination of controls by private monopolies; and in many respects this is a monopoly-ridden country. It is not a question of controls. It is a question of what kind of controls, by whom, and for whose benefit?
I say that the job of this house is to protect the public and to see that beneficial controls in the public interest are maintained, and as I said a little earlier, extended, if needs be, in the interests of the people and under the supervision of the elected representatives of the people. I know that such controls may embody new techniques of decentralization and democracy, which will enlarge the economic freedom and the social well-being of the people, which surely are the fundamentals of democratic progress.
At the moment we as a party are interested in preventing the removal of price ceilings and price controls, so that the cost of production and the standards of living shall not be affected adversely by price increases. The time will come of course, on the other hand, when the welfare of the Canadian people may be affected by quite the opposite thing; that is, by deflation. When that time comes the people of Canada will again demand the use of controls to prevent impoverishment of great masses of the people from an entirely different cause. As the minister has shown us tonight, our experience during the war when severe shortages of consumer goods existed, as well as in this immediate post-war period, has proved conclusively to the people of this country that public controls and subsidies can be used for the common good. But, as the minister has done tonight, the government on numerous occasions has made it clear that its aim is to dispense with controls in an orderly fashion and as rapidly as the situation will permit.
I wish to put our position in this way. On the other hand, we believe that the world situation and our own domestic situation demand the retention of public controls so that we may eventually stabilize our economy and proceed to expand and improve our own
Emergency Powers

standard of living. May I say that, in discussing this problem, we cannot overlook the world situation. The clock cannot be turned back. There is no going back again to the conditions that we knew, I was going to say, in the years before the war. I hope we may never see the conditions we saw in the nineteen-thirties. But what I wish to say is that we shall not see the world return to the kind of economic conditions it knew either before the first great war or between the two great wars.
The improvement of the standards of living for the people should be the aim and obligation of public economic policy; but this requires-and I want to say this emphatically -intelligent planning, and there can be no planning without measures of control. Some of my hon. friends object to planning; they object to controls; yet time and again these same objectors in this house rise in their places and demand the setting of parity prices for farm products, or the elimination of the grain exchange, or the marketing of wheat through a public agency such as the wheat board, and support plans for import and export boards. I wish to say that every one of these policies demands economic planning, and they all demand large measures of control. To secure and maintain proper relationship between the farmer's products and the things he must buy to produce them, and to live decently, requires the planning and control of a very wide area of our economic activity. The trouble is that some people want it both ways, and we cannot have it both ways. We cannot one day demand parity and orderly marketing, and the next day denounce public planning and controls as steps toward regimentation and slavery, as my hon. friend the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low) did in this house during the debate on the address.
Now I wish to say this because we want io put our position clearly before this house, because we believe in social planning and social security-

I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):
That Mr. Speaker do not now leave the chair but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the headlong decontrol policy of the government has depressed the standard of living of the people, threatens the country with economic chaos, and is surrendering the future of Canada to profiteering and monopoly;
And be it further resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to the introduction of a system of orderly and democratic controls so as to provide stable price levels and equitable price relationships in order to eliminate the injustices which now exist and to arrest the rapidly rising cost of living.
I have said that in the kind of economy in which we live, an economy still largely unaffected by the world trend toward social ownership, public controls may and will also involve the payment of subsidies. Again, subsidies involve quite comprehensive planning. Last August, for example, this house agreed that subsidies are desirable. It voted by a substantial majority, for example, for the continuation of the milk subsidy, a decision which the decontrol policy being followed forced the government to disobey. The wartime subsidy policj' proved a beneficial phase of our economic planning. In a broadcast over the CBC network on November 8 of last year Mr. Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, said:
The subsidy system under price control is aimed to keep down the cost of raw materials at the earliest stage of manufacture. This, in turn, prevents one rising price from feeding upwards to another, as it would otherwise do, because each manufacturer or wholesaler or retailer who handles the goods adds a percentage of the cost to him, as his profits.
Consequently, the higher the price the higher the profit mark-up which is based on a percentage of cost and so the higher the final price to you. That is why the collective saving made by all you consumers far exceeds the amount of the subsidy which is, of course, paid by you collectively as taxpayers.
And a government official, as was mentioned in this house some time ago, stated that for every dollar spent on price control the Canadian consumer had saved at least 855. In commenting on that statement when it was brought to his attention, on February 21 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said he did not vouch for the accuracy of the $55, but he could say he was sure the money spent on price controls had saved the Canadian con-

sumer substantial sums. Yet now the government and the minister are abandoning one control after another. Prices rise and the cost of living goes up. No wonder farmers are worried about their costs of production and farm prices and labour is anxious about current wage levels. Just a year ago the day before yesterday, March 18, 1946, gasoline prices were allowed to go up two cents a gallon. A month later, on April 15, farm machinery was permitted to advance by 12J per cent. Both these increases were criticized by my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party and the Social Credit group as well 3-3 by ourselves. Yet they wanted then, as they want now, the speedy removal of all controls; and let me remind them that was before the spectacular increase in prices of farm products in the United States.

I want to go on and say that Lammot du Pont, chairman of du Pont, wrote to Lord McGowan, chairman of Imperial Chemicals, stipulating that Canadian Industries must stay in Canada and not expand by exporting its products except upon terms satisfactory to du Pont and McGowan. That letter is also on the record.
Controls-yes, indeed, the campaign against public controls is in reality a smoke-screen behind which the Canadian economy can be handed over to powerful monopolistic interests. You say that chemicals are an exception. What of aluminum? What of steel? What of farm machinery? You will say that there are three firms manufacturing farm machinery and therefore there must be competition. I was a member of the agriculture committee which held an investigation in 1937 or 193S into farm machinery prices. Read that report and you will find that the manufacturers charged the same price for the same type of machine. We found that prices were usually set after the most powerful company, the International Harvester Company, had published its prices.
What of the packing industry? Again you will say that there is competition. According to the price spreads report, two companies control some eighty-five per cent of the business with one company, Canada Packers, controlling some fifty per cent.
Yes; hon. gentlemen are opposed to controls that attempt to control the prices and profits of these corporations. They call corporation control, free enterprise. Whose enterprise? How free is it? No wonder that Canada is often said to be monopoly ridden and, be it noted, by foreign monopolies at that! Not that I think a native monopoly is any better for the people than a foreign one. We want to see the elimination of that kind of control. We want to see the elimination of speculative agencies in foodstuffs like the grain exchange. We want to see the marketing of wheat continued under a public agency. And I say, because we want to do these things, they involve both planning and control.

Emergency Powers
Now to secure a proper relationship between the price of the farmer's products and the things he must buy to produce them and live decently, we require a comprehensive system of planning. And so, Mr. Speaker, I have taken this opportunity, because I think it should be done in all honesty and fairness to ourselves and in fairness to the country, to place before this house in the plainest of plain terms exactly where we stand in regard to controls.
We believe that democracy must extend its own power; we believe that democracy must be made to function; we believe that this political democracy which we possess is valuable and must be safeguarded. The right to free speech, the right to think, the right to elect freely our representatives in our democratic institutions, the right to freedom in religion-these things must be safeguarded. But we shall never have full democracy until we have economic democracy, until the producer through his own cooperative effort, or through the effort of his elected representatives, in the legislation which they enact, is given an opportunity to control and enjoy with his fellow man and woman the products of their own cooperative toil.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say only a few words with respect to this resolution and to voice my objection to the procedure which has been followed and to the method, the routine, of bringing this legislation before the house. I have neither the time nor have I the researches necessary to permit me to discuss this question of procedure from the constitutional point of view, or even from the point of view of the rules of the house. But from the point of view of custom and usage, I respectfully submit to the minister, and the ministry, that this is a most unprecedented resolution.
In the ordinary course, when it is proposed to ask parliament to appropriate money, resolutions are introduced asking for the appropriation of specific sums of money. The estimates, which are familiar to all of us, carry a list of some 600 or 700 items, and each one of those items is a resolution of this house. The sacrosanct formula used by the chairman of committees is something like this: "Resolved that a sum not exceeding"-let us say $3,000- "be voted for the construction of a wharf at"- such-and-such a place. So that all expenditures of money must be preceded by a resolution. And in the normal course of events these resolutions specify what the amount of money is to be.
This resolution before us, in the name of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), states:
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure-
"A measure".
-to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war and to provide therein that the governor in council may appoint and fix the compensation of the officers, clerks and employees necessary for the administration of any order or regulation continued in force by the act and further to provide that certain officers, clerks and employees may continue to perform the duties for which they were previously appointed.
The legislation which will be offered when this resolution passes will be offered, as I understand it, in the form of a schedule to the bill. This schedule, according to the minister's statement of yesterday, contains some fifty-sevem pieces of legislation. As I understand it, by passing this resolution we are authorizing the ministry to spend unlimited sums of money on fifty-seven pieces of legislation.
And mark you, Mr. Speaker, those fifty-seven orders in council will form a body of legislation as great as that which is passed during the whole session of one parliament, or as great as that incorporated in the statutes of one session. We are asked to do this in the form of one bill.
As an aside, may I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and any member of the house: How will it be possible to discuss intelligently-and I am not talking about the particular bill-at one time, as is our duty as members of the house, fifty-seven bills, some of them more important and carrying the implication of new principles, new ideas and new thoughts such as we have never had introduced in this house before; some of them good, some of them bad, some of them indifferent, some of them unimportant, and some of them awful.

I have been hearing so much about following the British parliament. I am glad the minister gives me an opportunity of saying what I have been wanting to say for about ten years. During the last war, every time this side of the house or the government of the day did something, somebody rose on the other side of the house and said the British did not do it in that way. I am fed up with knowing what way the British do it, or do not do it, and I am not taking an example in administration from the present British government, even though I would have voted for the Labour party had I been in England.
Emergency Powers

I do not care what the British government did; I do not care what the Australian government did. I think we are here to legislate for Canada. We are to legislate according to principles which we have adopted. We have been a parliament here since 1867, and I do not know why we should slavishly follow the rules of any other parliament. I believe there is more free democracy yet in this country than there is in any other country on earth, not excepting England. And whether it be here or in Great Britain or in Australia, the representatives of the people sent here by the people to represent them and to discuss legislation have a duty to perform.
I contend; I assert, without fear of contradiction, that in this mass of legislation which is to be thrown at members of parliament it will be impossible to have intelligent discussion or intelligent debate on the issues that are before the house.
But to return to the question of the resolution and the financial involvement, can anybody tell me that it will be possible, or that there is the slightest chance of members of the House of Commons who are here to see that expenditure of the people's money is carried on in an orderly fashion being able to perform their duty with respect to expenditures, under the terms of this resolution? This resolution carries with it the acceptance by this house, in advance, of any expenditure under such things as the wartime prices and trade board regulations. Probably they are not very important; I do not know; I do not think anybody knows; I do not think the minister knows. It carries with it such things as this, the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Incorporated. This will become law when the bill is passed. It provides for the setting up of a company, and that company may purchase or otherwise acquire, sell or otherwise dispose of stores, transport, process or otherwise deal in or deal in any goods, wares or merchandise. There is no limit. This Commodity Prices Stabilization Company can buy any goods, anything in this country, and we give them a blank cheque to do it.
We are setting up a crown company to be known as the Canadian Sugar Stabilization Company. I do not know how much money is involved in that or what the chances are of making a gain or a loss, but there are large sums involved, and so on all through the piece. Not one of these measures but at least merits, both from the financial point of view and from the point of view of principle, the most careful consideration of this house and at least 
some knowledge by hon. members of the amounts of money which might possibly be involved.
To return to the matters involved in the bill, I come to the question of controls. I am not prepared to say that I am opposed to all controls, nor am I in favour of all controls. I think it would be most unfair for any hon. member to say that those who oppose this resolution oppose controls as such. I would be quite willing to vote for any of the controls that we have at the present time. Like the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I too have some objection to the so-called free enterprise controlled by private industry, but I will not go as far as he does and have the totalitarian system of control which he would like. I believe it is possible for hon. members, it is possible for the people of Canada, to devise some means whereby we shall not take on the pattern of the totalitarian fascist controls as they exist in some countries in Europe, whereby we shall not return to the old system of control by private interests to the detriment of the common people.

That is what we are
waiting for.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
I know we are waiting for
it and I think thousands of people are struggling to attain it. I do not know that they have attained it as yet, but I am not prepared even today to take on holus-bolus, because the members of the government have not thought it out or because we have not been able to evolve a system, to admit that there is no middle course and that there is no means of having controls controlled by parliament.
I object to bureaucratic controls by people outside parliament. I have less objection- and in that I do not share the opinion of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker)

and we are almost forced to the conclusion, in order to do away with bureaucratic control, to give more controls to the ministers of the crown and to the members of the administration. If I am to be kicked around I want to be kicked around by someone I can see and hear and kick back and not by someone surrounded by a steel or iron curtain in some office of the government whom I never see. I say that, Mr. Speaker, without in any way wishing to criticize any of the existing controllers or those of the past. The few times when, at the request of my constituents, I had business with the controllers I had the fairest

Emergency Powers
and most courteous treatment, and that applies to Donald Gordon as well as to all the others.
I could, I suppose, except that it is pretty late and it may not be fair, quote a precedent with respect to bills of this kind. In my recollection there was only one piece of legislation like it, namely, that introduced by Mr. Bennett in 1931 and 1932. To that piece of legislation men now sitting on this side of the house took strenuous objection. It is within the memory of many of us sitting here that we objected to the first reading of the resolution, right up to the closing. At that time there was presented to us a bill called "unemployment and farm relief." The objection taken by the members of the opposition of that day was that the two things, unemployment and farm relief should not be provided for in the same resolution. I wonder whether we ever thought then that some day we ourselves would be bringing in a bill with fifty-seven different varieties of legislation.
I shall not quote the arguments used by the members of the opposition of that day; but I think if anyone will look over them they will find that if there was one thing that the opposition asked for it was that the resolution mention the specific amounts of money that were to be expended on each of these subjects. It was a blank cheque and members of the opposition objected strenuously to any legislation involving a blank cheque. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is a blank cheque which involves more important considerations than any blank cheque has ever been given in this country.
I would appeal to the minister once more to try to break down this legislation into its component parts. It would be possible to do that. In looking it over, I find the civil service commission mentioned. There are five orders in council all dealing with preference to returned soldiers. That has no place in this kind of legislation. One of the orders in council is simply an order providing that the people who served in the war of 19391945 should have the same preference with regard to civil service positions as those who served in the war of 1914-1918. Why introduce that in such an extraordinary piece of legislation as this? We may question the conditions with respect to time, with respect to age and in any other respect under which these positions and this preference will be made available to all veterans, but I have never heard in this house or outside it anyone questioning the fact that the veterans of the last war should have the same preference
with regard to the civil service as the veterans of the first war. I submit that there is no necessity for bringing in this sort of legislation in a resolution which involves-

They would lose the

speechtext:
I hear my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) whispering to my hon. friend the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) that he is having a committee and bringing in a bill. Let him bring in a bill; he has until May 15. But do not let him load down legislation and make it an affront to parliament, as this thing is, giving us something that we cannot possibly study and discuss. The people of Canada will not understand what the whole argument is about.
There are a dozen other things in this. There is the pelagic sealing treaty. I do not know anything about it, but I do not think it has its place in a piece of legislation dealing with the wartime prices and trade bo&rd, or dealing with the stabilization fund or dealing with the control of sugar, lumber and steel. There are other matters dealing with compensation for merchant seamen, and there are, I understand, certain endeavours to wind up the war service gratuity.
All these things could be dealt with in their place and passed by this house in five minutes, but I object to these almost innocuous and certainly easily explained pieces of legislation being thrown in with pieces of legislation on the principles of which the people of this country and the members of this parliament are not agreed.
My last objection is that, by passing this resolution and bringing in the bill, in the shape in which it will be brought in, we are creating an extremely dangerous precedent. We are preparing the way for the time when any government or a government which will not have the same respect for ancient constitutional usages and practices will be in power in this country, and when they come in they will have ready-made at their hand such legislation as will enable them at once to put into effect their theories and the practice in which they believe.
I have said before and said many a time that I have no objection to a great many of their theories. I would like to see many of them put into practice if they could do away with the regimentation that goes with them. But I certainly do not want to be a member of a party which will prepare the way and make it easier for them when they do come into power to carry out what I believe to be
Emergency Powers

false principles in a democracy. In other words, I do not want to be a St. John the Baptist for a socialist messiah.

A motion to refer a bill, resolution or any question to the committee of the whole, or any standing or special committee shall preclude all amendment of the main question.

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency . . .
And so on; and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar moved as an amendment:
That Mr. Speaker do not now leave the chair hut that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the headlong decontrol policy of the government has depressed the standard of living of the people, threatens the country with economic chaos, and is surrendering the future of Canada to profiteering and monopoly;
And be it further resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to the introduction of a system of orderly and democratic controls so as to provide stable price levels and equitable price relationships in order to eliminate the injustices which now exist and to arrest the rapidly rising cost of living.

In my opinion the "yeas" have it. Call in the members.
Mr. SPEAKER put the question as follows:
The question before the house is an appeal from the Speaker's ruling. Mr. Ilsley moved, seconded by Mr. Mackenzie, the following motion:
That the Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war and to provide therein that the governor in council may appoint and fix the compensation of the officers, clerks and employees necessary for the administration of any order or regulation continued in force by the Act and further to provide that certain officers, clerks and employees may continue to perform the duties for which they yrere previously appointed.
Mr. Coldwell moved, seconded by Mr. Maclnnis, in amendment:
That Mr. Speaker do not now leave the-chair but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the headlong decontrol policy of the government has depressed the standard of living of the people, threatens the country with economic chaos, and is surrendering the future of Canada to profiteering and monopoly
And be it further resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to the introduction of a system of orderly and democratic controls so as to provide stable price levels and equitable price relationships in order to eliminate the injustices which now exist and to arrest the rapidly rising cost of living.
I declared the amendment out of order, and I based my ruling on standing order 50, which reads as follows:
A motion to refer a bill, resolution or any other question to the committee of the whole, or any standing or special committee shall preclude all amendment of the main question.
The house divided on the question:	Shall
the Speaker's decision be sustained? And the decision of the chair was sustained on the following division:
